digest.intro: Satellites stalking satellites, neurons turning legible, and epistemic poisoning goes mainstream.

items.title: France imposes curfews after 550,000 take to the streets
items.blurb: What started as protests over deteriorating school conditions has metastasized into nationwide unrest over fuel prices and gutted public services — 2,500 arrests, two deaths, 1,000 injured officers, and hundreds of millions in business damage later. Italy is planning troop deployments as their own protests widen. The interior minister offered his resignation; Macron refused it.

items.title: Russian satellite stalks Ukraine's imaging bird to within 500 meters
items.blurb: Kosmos 2612 spent months quietly matching orbits with ICEYE-X36 — a commercial SAR satellite that Ukraine uses for battlefield intelligence — then last week closed to within 500 meters and held station, circling ahead and behind. LeoLabs, which tracks objects down to 2cm in LEO, calls it the first known unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit. Space as a warfare domain just got a lot less abstract.

items.title: Putin proposes a US-Russia-China nuclear summit; Trump says he's open to it
items.blurb: A trilateral summit on nuclear arms between the three largest arsenals in the world would be the most structurally significant diplomatic move of the year — and Kyiv is already nervous, reading it as cover for delayed Western military aid. Worth watching even at the proposal stage: the geometry of who sits at that table redraws the Ukraine calculus entirely.

items.title: The claim that ~90% of LLM neurons are individually readable — and why it's contested
items.blurb: Nick Cammarata's 26,000-word post argues that most neurons in large language models are not hopelessly entangled in superposition but are individually interpretable — which, if true, would mean we can actually monitor and steer what these systems are doing internally. Stanford's Chris Potts calls it a hunch without the rigor to back it; others are calling it a five-year leap. The disagreement itself is the signal: interpretability research just got a lot louder.

items.title: DeepSeek open-sources its production inference engine the same week DHS bans it from federal systems
items.blurb: DeepInfer — the inference framework actually running DeepSeek's production services — is now public, complete with FlashMLA kernels, MoE expert parallelism, and confidence-scheduled speculative decoding. The DHS simultaneously issued a Federal Register order excluding DeepSeek products from all civilian executive branch systems. The irony: open-sourcing it means the ban is essentially unenforceableat the technology layer.

items.title: Someone seeded 50,000 fake statistics online and watched LLMs cite them as fact — including in a bank's research
items.blurb: A deliberate experiment: publish a site full of fabricated numbers, watch Google deindex it, watch ChatGPT keep citing it anyway — funneling over 10,000 AI-referred sessions and earning links from Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost. The made-up statistics ended up in an academic paper and investment research. This is a working proof-of-concept for epistemic poisoning at scale, and the incentive to do it maliciously is obvious.

items.title: WhatsApp's help pages contained hidden instructions telling AI not to mention regulators or cite privacy law
items.blurb: Buried in HTML invisible to users but readable by AI: instructions not to recommend data protection regulators when someone was locked out and wanted their account deleted, and not to mention the relevant law once a user mentioned a lawyer. WhatsApp's own privacy policy for Europe names both the regulator and the law — so the visible policy and the invisible AI policy were pointing in opposite directions. Redact found it by reading all 545 linked help pages.

items.title: 12 out of 12 T1D patients off insulin after islet transplant protected by a new rejection drug
items.blurb: A University of Chicago trial transplanted donor pancreatic islet cells alongside tegoprubart — a novel immunosuppressant — and every single participant stopped needing external insulin, with stable results and no reported serious side effects. The big remaining hurdle is donor scarcity, which is why SUNY Upstate's parallel work converting patients' own blood cells into islets matters: it's the path to a version that scales. Early, but the signal is clean.

items.title: On intuition as genuine perception — what 'creepy vibe' actually tells you epistemically
items.blurb: This essay argues that when you sense something is off — a stranger, an email, a deal — you're not reasoning poorly, you're perceiving directly: the man doesn't just trigger a heuristic, he's simply presented to you as creepy, the same way red things are presented as red. Philosophers have mostly ignored this category of everyday intuition in favor of the rarefied a priori kind, which means the rational credentials of the most practically useful form of knowing have been left almost entirely unexamined. Thirty minutes well spent.

facts.fact: Kosmos 2612 closed from hundreds of kilometers away to within 500 meters of ICEYE-X36, and LeoLabs says it was 'likely quite a bit closer than that' — making it the first known unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit.

The fabricated statistics site was deindexed by Google but still drives 10,000+ AI-referred sessions, earned links from Shopify and DHL, and got cited in both an academic paper and a bank's investment research — seven months after launch.

Disney acquired most of Character.AI's staff and technology while the company filed for bankruptcy specifically so the legal shell — not Disney — retains liability for the multiple active lawsuits over chatbot harm to minors.

WhatsApp's AI help chatbot was secretly instructed not to recommend data protection regulators to locked-out users, while WhatsApp's own visible privacy policy for Europe explicitly names those same regulators and the law granting users the right to complain to them.

All 12 participants in the University of Chicago islet transplant trial stopped needing external insulin — 12 out of 12 — after receiving donor islets protected by a new rejection drug called tegoprubart.

make_something.prompt: Build a small web sketch where motion leaves a trail — something moves across the canvas and its recent path subtly warps or displaces the objects it passed near, as if space has a short memory. Inspired by the Current Biology finding that primate IT cortex shifts object position codes based on recent visual history, while AI vision stays pixel-rigid. The constraint: no object should ever be where the math says it strictly is — only where it seems to be given what just happened.

art_picks.title: Decasia
art_picks.creator: Bill Morrison
art_picks.why: Found footage assembled entirely from decaying nitrate film — Morrison treats entropy itself as a collaborator, and the result is one of the most formally radical films ever made about time, material, and the image as physical object. If you care about what surfaces remember, this one haunts.

art_picks.title: Agnes Martin: Paintings and Drawings
art_picks.creator: Agnes Martin
art_picks.why: Martin spent decades making near-invisible grid paintings that sit at the exact intersection of system and sensation — the rules are rigid, the feeling is oceanic. Her work is about what happens when you submit completely to a structure, and it rewards slow looking in a way almost nothing else does.

art_picks.title: Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill
art_picks.creator: Grouper
art_picks.why: Liz Harris makes music that sounds like it was recorded inside a memory — tape hiss, voice, guitar, all processed into something that barely holds together. It's the rarest kind of record: technically primitive, emotionally precise, and completely its own world. The physical/digital blur is baked into the texture itself.

events.name: Animal Collective – Feels Live (21st Anniversary)
events.why: Two-night run where Animal Collective play their 2005 LP Feels in full — a rare chance to hear one of the most formally strange and emotionally open albums of the 2000s performed live, in a venue that was literally an old industrial building.

events.name: Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio
events.why: The Atelier Brancusi in Paris is closed for the Centre Pompidou renovation — so its rarely-lent sculptures, hand-carved furniture, tools, films, and photographs are all at MoMA on the sixth floor, reconstructing the studio-as-artwork. Once in a generation.

events.name: Ai Weiwei: Illumination
events.venue: Vito Schnabel Gallery, 455 W 19th St, Chelsea
events.why: Opening night for Ai Weiwei at Vito Schnabel — worth catching at the opening before it gets crowded; Weiwei's work operates as mythology and political object simultaneously, which is rare territory.

events.name: SHELLRAISER – LiveCodeNYC October Algorave
events.why: LiveCodeNYC's monthly algorave: musicians write and modify generative code live on-screen while the music plays, collapsing the distance between authorship, system, and performance — the code is projected, the crowd watches the source.
